author: Autodesk
description: Procedurally construct a skeleton with a spine and arms, compute its animation. Additionally, get the head joint data to drive the motion of the head mesh.

metadata.author: Autodesk
metadata.description: Procedurally construct a skeleton with a spine and arms, compute its animation. Additionally, get the head joint data to drive the motion of the head mesh.

_notes.text:
Utilizing the data from the skeleton's joints, we generate their animation procedurally within ***compute_wave_animation***. 

Subsequently, we use the computed matrices to transform all skeleton joints using ***transform_joints*** which updates the full joint transformation data from user specified matrices, in this case, operator matrices. This means we can retrieve the ***joint_world_matrix*** downstream without needing to compute it since transforming joints computes or updates all transformation components.

You can play with the ***Animation Settings*** parameters to alter the wave animation, and visualize the result using ***skeleton_scope***.

Procedurally compute the skeleton's joint data. We initiate by determining the spine joint data, followed by calculating and appending data each arm. This data is then used to construct the actual skeleton object. Detailed explanations on the computation process are available in the compounds below.
Update additional joint data to be used to compute the procedural animation inside the ***compute_wave_animation*** compound on the right.

To determine the matrix of the spine's tip joint without relying on names or paths, we utilize the fact that the first chain in this skeleton represents the spine joints. Thus, the first joint without chidren is the tip of the spine.

To find it, we update the ***joint_children_indices*** geo property, which is a per point array of indices to the children joints. We then get the size of all sub arrays and search for the first one that has a size of 0, meaning that it does not have any children.

Create a sphere positioned at the origin. We create the sphere with ***base_to_pivot*** enabled so that its base is set at the origin. We then assign it a diagnostic material so that the mesh is colored in red. Finally, we transform the mesh points by the head joint's world matrix that we just got before.
You can play with the unconnected input parameters like ***spine_joint_count,  arm_count, steps_between_levels***, to modify the shape and topology of the dancing skeleton.

_backdrops.title: Create joint data and construct skeleton
Create and apply animation matrices on skeleton
Create sphere, assign color, transform mesh to joint to
Create head sphere and place it on tip joint
Compute and append arms' joints data

_notes.text:
Create an array of pivot matrices that represents the skeleton's spine.

Additionally, we calculate their orientation ensuring the secondary joint rotation axis (***Y*** in this case) faces Z+. This orientation facilitates applying the procedural animation predominantly around this axis in subsequent steps.

Calculate the parent indices for the spine joints. Given that the spine joints are initially set in the skeleton, we designate the first value as the ***invalid_index***, marking it as the root joint. For the following joints, we set the values as ***current_index - 1***, ensuring that each joint's predecessor in the array serves as its parent.

The formula to compute the rotation radians animation.

***sin(ratios * frequency + speed * seconds * 2PI) * magnetudes***
Use the input axis ***local_rotation_axis*** and the computed radians to compose an operator transformation matrix.

We know that the first joint chain of our skeleton represents  the spine. Accordingly, we use ***joint_chain_index*** with values equal to ***0*** to set the spine joints' magnetude values. For other index values, we set the magnetude values for the arm joints.

Utilizing the ***joint_depth*** values, we calculate the absolute ratios representing a joint's position within the entire hierarchy. A value of ***0.0*** indicates the joint is at the root level, while a value of ***1.0*** signifies it is the deepest joint within the hierarchy.

_backdrops.title: Compute per joint ratios and magnetudes
Compute joint absolute ratios from depth values
Set different magnetudes for the spine and for the arms

_notes.text:
When calculating both arms on the same hierarchy level, we aim for the left and right arms to share the same parent spine joint. This is achieved by dividing the ***current_index*** by two, ensuring both joints use the same parent.

Additionally, when determining arm joint positions and orientations, the method varies based on the side we're working on. Hence, we employ a modulo operation to alternate between the right and left sides.

_backdrops.title: Get current arm's parent joint index
Append current arm's joint data in global arrays

_notes.text: Just like with the spine joints, calculate the orientations for the arm joints to ensure the secondary joint rotation axis (***Y+*** in this case) faces ***Z+***. The distinction here is that we aim the primary axis towards either ***X-*** or ***X+***, based on which side is currently being computed.

Calculate the parent indices for the arm joints. This process is similar to what we did in ***create_spine_joint_data***. However, for the first arm joint, we set its parent index to the spine joint where we want the arm to attach.

Starting from the parent spine joint's position, we create the arm joints' positions. All joints are offseted localy by the ***arm_joint_length*** value, going toward either ***X-*** or ***X+*** Depending on which side we are computing.

_backdrops.title: Compute current arm's joint parent index values

_notes.text: For every pair of arms, we assign spine joint indices as the parent indices for the initial joint in their chains. Beginning at the top of the spine, we progressively move downward based on the ***steps_between_levels*** value.

_backdrops.title: Get first arm joints' parent indices
